text: This page records how the pricing was built and why each choice was made, in five steps per market. The actuary gave the direction: the order of work, the rules, the checks to run, the key challenges to the results and every final decision. AI agents executed the work inside those rules and proposed alternatives.

Part 1: (1) data — what is in the tables, how they were cleaned and how the target was built like a reserve; (2) model — the judge first, then every model tested and the final choice. Part 2: (3) compare the two markets; (4) select the model on a bench fixed in advance; (5) price and limits. Tab 6 shows how AI was used and checked.

Every decision starts from an instruction or a check the actuary asked for, or from a finding the AI reported. Each one lists the evidence, the alternative that was rejected, the decision and its measured effect, with the file where the work is.

Instructions are how the work was steered. Checks requested are verifications the actuary asked for before accepting a result. AI findings are issues the agents raised on their own, then confirmed with a test before anything changed.

The data are eleven tables of a fictitious insurer: motor, buildings and contents policies with one row per policy per year, their claims, customers, addresses and yearly weather per address. The claims table has no row id: every claim is placed in its policy row by policy number and loss date.
Part 2 has the same structure for an emerging market with two policy years instead of four, plus an expense table and twenty reference policies to quote an office premium.

Every column has a status. Used columns enter the frequency model of each peril and the boosting model; rebuilt columns are replaced by a cleaner version (age instead of date of birth, exposure from the dates). Keys only join tables.

Excluded columns fall into three groups. Leakage: customer-service contacts are generated by the claims themselves, and the renewal decision is made after the period and is absent from the test. Decoys: about thirty columns with no effect once the true drivers are in, verified per peril with the generator reconstruction and with residual checks. Other exclusions: the written premium (today's tariff, circular) and columns with no risk logic such as surname and e-mail domain.
An automated test fails the build if any excluded column reaches a model.

A value is corrected only when the data themselves prove it wrong: dates that contradict the exposure, a code that finds no customer, an amount a thousand times the median. Where there is no way to know which value is right, the row is flagged and left as it is. Every rule is the same for training and test, and the original value stays next to the corrected one.

The table also keeps what was tried and dropped: the zero-mileage rule that the data contradicted, and the loss-date correction that did not improve the judges. The Part 2 rows show that the emerging market had the same defects, fixed by the same code through one configuration file.

Frequency and average claim cost per peril, developed market against emerging market, on reported claims capped at the large-loss threshold. The emerging book has more glass, storm and third-party claims and much smaller bodily-injury claims; reporting delays are almost identical, which is what allowed the development to be borrowed.

Almost every row has no claim, and a few claims are worth a great deal: the median claim is a fraction of the 99.9th percentile. This is why the metric is a Tweedie deviance and why a single large claim must not decide the level of a line.

There is no column with the 2025 cost of a row. What the data show is the incurred cost at 31/12/2024 of rows from 2021 to 2024. The target is built like a reserve: reported cost, plus claims not yet reported (IBNR), plus the development of open claims (IBNER), brought to the 2025 level with a trend per peril, with large claims capped and their excess spread as a load.

Share of claims reported within a given number of days, per peril. Glass, theft and fire are reported within days; bodily injury and subsidence take months to years. Delays are estimated with a reverse-time estimator for right-truncated data: counting the delays visible at 31/12/2024 would understate them, because recent slow claims are not yet visible.
From this curve each row gets a completeness π, the share of its claims expected to be reported already. A 2024 motor row has seen only about 57% of its bodily-injury claims.

Cost per exposure year by accident year: reported, at ultimate, and at the 2025 level. Reported cost falls for the youngest years only because they are young. Once developed and trended, every year should cost about the same; a slope by origin year is the test that the trend is right.

Trends are estimated per peril for frequency and for average cost, with a regression on the accident years. A frequency trend that is not significant falls back to the line's trend when that one is significant, otherwise to zero; weather perils get no frequency trend because the model uses the 2025 weather directly. Severity keeps its own estimate even when it is not significant: borrowing the median of the line's significant perils gave bodily injury the 8.0% of short-tail perils and over-trended the motor level.

Claims are capped near the 99.9th percentile and the excess is spread as a load per exposure year. Without the cap one open bodily-injury claim of 11.9 million would be 55% of the whole motor excess and would set the level of the line.

The structure was tested before a model was chosen. For each peril an additive frequency model was compared with one allowing interactions; the additive one is as good or better in 14 of 15 perils. Severity is almost constant per peril with a few drivers. The model is therefore frequency × severity per peril, additive, plus experience rating on each policy's own history, blended with one boosting model written by the local AI.

D² of the frequency model per peril, fitted on 2021–23 and scored on 2024: additive (one split per tree, a log-linear model with free curves) against interactions (fifteen leaves). The labels are the main drivers found for each peril.

One-way analysis, as in tariff work: for one variable, the observed cost per exposure year by class and what each model predicts out of sample. When the curves have the same shape and direction, the models give the variable the same meaning. A decoy can still show a slope: the model does not use it, but it is correlated with true drivers.

Experience rating multiplies each policy's price by (N + k) / (E + k), where N is the claims the policy had and E the claims the model expected over the same history. With no claims the factor drifts below one as expected claims build up; each claim lifts it. Motor uses k = 16 after the judges disagreed on k = 8 and the official judge, the frozen holdout and the public board agreed.

How much of the error can any model remove? Tweedie deviance splits into noise plus the distance between the prediction and the true mean. A simulation calibrated on our data says most of the deviance is pure noise; our out-of-sample score matches a perfect model with the same information, so effort went into the target and the history rather than into model complexity.

Every Part 1 submission, by date. The steps that moved the score were actuarial: the per-peril structure, experience rating and the final fit on all policies. Below that level public differences were noise, so later choices were made on the internal judges. The private scores (second colour), revealed after the competition closed: they sit above the public ones and follow the same steps, but the small public differences at the top did not carry over.

Every model fitted in Part 1, scored on the same two time folds (fit 2021–22 → score 2023, fit 2021–23 → score 2024) with the official judge, all lines pooled. The chart shows the mean of the two folds; the table and the tooltip give each year and each line. Models that never reached a submission are drawn hollow: most of the work was trying alternatives and keeping only what beat the simpler model. The level of these scores is higher than Kaggle's because the target has large losses capped; only the differences between models matter.

Three things stand out. Frequency × severity per peril beats every direct model once it has the right structure. Experience rating lifts every family by a similar amount. The GLM, the elastic net and the neural CANN are close to the main model but highly correlated with it, so they took no weight in the blend; the Qwen boosting model is the only partner that added something.

Each dot is one model, in the order its out-of-fold predictions were produced (dates below), scored on the judge chosen above; the line is the best score so far. Filled dots were submitted, hollow ones were tried and dropped, the ringed ones are in the final blend. The curve climbs in three steps (per-peril structure, experience rating, the final pipeline) and is flat in between: most of the work was alternatives that did not beat the simpler model.
All models are scored on the final target, so earlier models are judged by the same rules as the last ones.

Choosing between models needs a judge, and the truth for the recent years has to be built. The official judge imitates Kaggle, but spreading IBNR over every row rewards flat models. So each decision was read on three judges: official for the level, own (reported claims against prediction × completeness) for the shape, and true large losses for their allocation. A frozen 10% holdout, a paired bootstrap and the public board were checks, never targets.

The rule, fixed on 20 October: a change is kept only if it improves both years on the official and own judges. When the judges disagree, the own judge decides the shape and the disagreement is written down.

Cases where the judges were consulted: the change in deviance on each judge (×10⁻⁴ on the line, fold 2023 / fold 2024) and the decision. The motor credibility case is the only one where the judges contradicted each other significantly; the actuary chose k = 16 because official, holdout and public agreed.

A local model, Qwen 27B, ran on the actuary's Mac: the data never left the machine and every experiment cost no tokens. It worked in Karpathy-style autoresearch loops. Each loop has one file Qwen may edit, a program that says what to try and what not to touch, and a frozen judge it cannot modify that scores both validation years. A change is kept only if the worse of the two years improves; otherwise the file is rolled back.

Guardrails refuse code that reads the validation target, imports modules or changes the function's contract. Nothing Qwen kept went into a submission until it was re-run on the three judges (Part 1) or the seven-check bench (Part 2). This two-stage design is deliberate: hundreds of attempts on the same two folds invite luck (the same problem as p-hacking), so the loop's own judge only filters, and the few survivors are re-scored on the three judges and the frozen holdout before they count. The Qwen models that reached a submission are in the chart above, with every other model, on all three judges; the one that passed is the boosting partner in the final Part 1 model below.

Qwen had three roles. It searched for better models overnight; it independently re-derived the actuary's conclusions, which made them more credible; and it reviewed the pipeline code before Part 2 (see 6 · AI and governance).

Each dot is one experiment written by Qwen; the line is the best score kept so far. Most proposals are discarded, a few are blocked by guardrails or crash, and the kept steps are where the line moves. In the main loop the big jumps come from dropping raw make_model (iteration 23) and from shallow trees that enforce an additive structure (iteration 73), the same structure the actuary had found by reconstructing the generator.
Every change Qwen kept in the Part 1 loops, in its own words, and what happened to it afterwards.

Before Part 2, Qwen read the pipeline looking for leakage, bugs and code that would break on a new market, then tried to refute each of its own high and medium findings. The few that survived were checked by hand: no leakage, and four real fragilities that the emerging market (other years, missing columns) would have hit.

The same pipeline ran on the emerging market with one configuration file. The automated audit listed what changed: two years of data, new regions, gender, ages only in bands, no credit band, mileage or telematics, a hotter climate, and a 2025 book that is three-quarters new business from a broker.
The Part 1 model is the prior; the emerging data set the level and only the corrections they can support. Every correction had to pass a seven-check bench fixed in advance.

The 2025 book is three-quarters new business: a portfolio the insurer took over from a broker at the start of the year. Those policies have no claims yet, so no model can be fitted or tuned on them, and tuning on the public third of the test would be fitting noise. What can be checked is whether they look like the policies the model and the new-business correction were estimated on.

They do. A classifier asked to tell the broker policies apart from the emerging new business of 2023–24, using every rating variable, does no better than chance (AUC 0.52–0.53). Their expected cost under the Part 1 prior is within 4% of the 2023–24 new business on every line (motor 760 against 787 per exposure year). Both are much riskier than renewals for visible reasons: 28% young drivers against 18%, fewer no-claims years. The model already prices that through the rating factors; the +19% new-business correction is what remains on top, and the broker book gives no reason to expect it to differ.
Because the two populations match, re-weighting the training data towards the broker book (the legitimate version of optimising on it) would change nothing.

Share of exposure by class for each population: the developed market, emerging renewals and new business of 2023–24, and the two parts of the 2025 book. The broker portfolio overlaps the emerging new business almost exactly; renewals are older, with more no-claims years.

Observed claim frequency and average claim cost (reported, capped at the large-loss threshold, not yet developed) per peril. Emerging motor has more claims than the developed market but much smaller ones. Within the emerging market, new business has both more and larger claims than renewals in raw terms; once age and no-claims years are taken into account the frequency difference disappears and what remains is severity, driven by five bodily-injury claims.

Fit on 2023, score on 2024: a model built only on the emerging data against the Part 1 prior with an emerging level. The prior wins on every line; a simulation of a small market inside the developed one agrees in 16 of 18 cases.

Backtest of the borrowed reporting curves: accident year 2023 seen at end-2023, developed with the Part 1 curves, against what was actually reported by end-2024. Filled dots: emerging market; open dots: the same test on the developed market.

Every idea tested on the bench, with the change in the shape judge and the own judge (×10⁻⁴) and the number of checks won out of seven. The rule was fixed before testing: keep a correction only if it wins at least five of seven on both.

The acquired broker portfolio: new business costs 19% more than renewals. Frequency is at par; the excess is severity from five bodily-injury claims. Public scores of the three variants agree with the internal sign, so the credibility-weighted correction stays, with its uncertainty stated.
Price change when one assumption moves. Motor is robust; buildings swing with the weight given to the 2023 fire year, so that uncertainty is stated with its price effect rather than tuned.

Two kinds of AI worked on the actuary's instructions and inside rules the actuary fixed. A coding agent rebuilt the target, wrote the pipeline, the judges and the diagnostics, and logged every step. A local model ran autonomous research loops overnight: it edits one file, a frozen judge it cannot modify scores both validation years, and a change is kept only if the worse year improves.
Nothing an AI produced entered a submission until it was re-run on the three judges (Part 1) or the seven-check bench (Part 2).
Outcome of every autonomous experiment by loop. Most proposals are discarded by the judge; guardrails block code that reads the validation target, imports modules or changes the function contract.

Public against private score of every Part 1 submission. The public board is a third of the test; gaps below 0.0005 on it were coin flips on the private board, which is why the leaderboard was used only as a final check.

Each dot is one Part 2 submission on the public third of the test. Candidates were built only from changes that had already passed the seven-check bench; probes changed one thing on purpose to learn about the test, and were never candidates. Every candidate since sub_07 sits within about 0.0005 of the others, below the public noise of about 0.0009: the bench, not the board, decided.

Two probes settled open questions. Moving any line's level by ±10% moved the score by at most 0.0007, so the gap to the top teams is about the shape of the prices, not their level. A flatter driver-experience curve, which our official-target judge liked and our own judge did not, lost 0.0014: the test behaves like real claims, and the rule that a change must pass both judges held.

The insurer's own premium turned out to carry the most useful local signal. In motor, the most expensive sixth of policies (almost all drivers aged 17–24 with no no-claims years) cost 19% less than the Part 1 prior predicts; the cheapest sixth cost more. Correcting for age, years licensed or no-claims years one by one did nothing on the bench; the premium, a single index of the local tariff, did. As a frequency correction it gained +18.2 / +11.7 (sub_19); inside the cost GLM it gained more (sub_21: +41.2 / +25.4 over the frequency form on a stricter bench, +0.0009 on the public board). It adds nothing in buildings and contents, where the Part 1 model that already used the relative premium became the prior instead. We found it late, on 27 October.

At the end every piece of the final model was re-checked on a stricter bench: fit on one year, score the other, with disjoint customers (six checks instead of seven partly overlapping ones). Every piece held; storm in buildings proved neutral, and the 10% emerging-only model in buildings helps in one direction of time and hurts in the other (the 2023 fire year).
The final model, step by step and line by line. Each step is kept only because it passed the bench; the column on the right says where it entered and what it gained.

The same loop design ran on the emerging market: Qwen could edit one file of corrections on top of the Part 1 prior, judged on 2023 → 2024. Of 124 experiments, its judge kept 4. None entered the final model as Qwen code: each kept idea was re-run on the seven-check bench or overlapped a correction already tested there.

Its value here was as an independent check. Working alone, it found a new-business correction in motor in the same direction as the one the bench accepted, and per-peril levels in buildings, of which the bench kept only storm. Qwen's Part 1 boosting model could not be carried over: it relies on columns the emerging market does not have (credit band, exact ages).
